extracted.intended_audience: homeowners, builders, and plumbers planning or installing residential plumbing and water-supply systems
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, prescriptive guidance for selecting, sizing, installing, and maintaining water-supply, storage, pumping, and drainage systems for a single house (including tanks, pumps, pipes, fixtures, and traps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider steam pump only if small boiler exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of a steam pump would probably not be considered for a single house unless a small boiler was already installed for other purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a boiler is already present (e.g., for dairy or silage work), it may be simple to connect a small duplex pump; consider one boiler operating different machinery when extensive improvements are contemplated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select pump capacity for required lift and head
rubrics_metrics.description: Pumps must be chosen with capacities and proportions appropriate to the head and required gallons per minute; tables of small-capacity pumps are provided showing piston diameters, strokes, revolutions, and gallons per minute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tabulated data (e.g., Table XIV) to match pump cylinder/piston/stroke to desired output and head; refer to manufacturer catalogues for specific models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid compressed-air lifts unless justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Compressed air is a source of power for raising water from deep wells but is neither economical in first cost nor in operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only consider air-lift systems if the advantage of avoiding in-well valves/mechanisms outweighs higher capital and operating costs; air lifts avoid having mechanism deep in well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tank material choice: iron preferred to wood for outdoor tanks
rubrics_metrics.description: If the tank is out of doors, protection against frost must be carefully attended to; wooden tanks are likely to rot and if left standing empty become leaky; they are less worth while than iron tanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer iron (galvanized) tanks for outdoor use; if wood is used inside, line with lead, copper, or galvanized iron to improve longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior tanks must be water-tight and well supported
rubrics_metrics.description: If the tank is to be placed inside a building, care must be taken to have it water-tight and to have the supports of the tank ample for the excessive weight imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 500-gallon attic tank weighs over two tons—support by truss or hang from rafters with iron straps bolted to tank and rafters; place over a partition carried through to the cellar if possible to avoid floor settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attic tank capacity equals daily consumption (minimum sizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The attic tank's capacity should be equal to the daily consumption of water; minimum size such that night flow will just fill the tank with day's needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use daily consumption as basis for calculation; a commonly suggested size ~500 gallons (approx. 4 ft cube) for domestic use but compute per actual consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attic tank overflow must discharge through roof with screen and flap
rubrics_metrics.description: An overflow is essential; best accomplished by carrying a pipe out through a hole in the roof, ample in size, provided with a screen at the inside end, and examined frequently to ensure it remains open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a light flap valve on overflow to keep out cold in winter; check overflow regularly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wooden attic tanks: construction and minimum material
rubrics_metrics.description: Wooden tanks should never be made of less than two-inch stuff and should not depend upon nails or screws alone for holding the sides together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Line wooden tanks with lead or sheet iron for water-tightness; paint metal lining at intervals to prevent rust; follow recommended assembly (e.g., Figure 56).

rubrics_metrics.name: Main supply pipe sizing: use 3/4-inch galvanized iron normally
rubrics_metrics.description: The main supply pipe, except when pressure is very great, is most satisfactory when made of three-quarter-inch galvanized iron. Even with a high pressure, half-inch pipe is unsatisfactory because of great velocity and premature packing wear in faucets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install a stop-and-waste valve just inside the cellar wall so the valve may be shut and pipes drawn off when house unoccupied; protect pipes from freezing—do not run directly in front of a window or along sills unless wrapped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate fixtures close together to save expense
rubrics_metrics.description: It is wise, in order to save expense, to have all these fixtures as close together as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: place laundry tub under kitchen sink and bath-room fixtures directly over the kitchen sink to minimize piping runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-water piping: return to bottom of boiler for circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Although not essential, it is desirable to carry the hot-water pipe back to the bottom of the hot-water boiler so that the circulation of hot water is maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids wasting water and waiting until hot water arrives at a faucet; hot-water pipe should be same size as main supply and of galvanized iron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-water branch placement at stove and circuit routing
rubrics_metrics.description: A branch must be taken off at the level of the kitchen stove and run into the hot-water boiler at or near the bottom. The house circuit is then run from the top of the boiler; a return pipe (if provided) should re-enter at the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a separate circulation circuit from the bottom of the hot-water tank to the water-back and back into the tank halfway up when using a water-back arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faucet type: prefer screw-down valves for reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest, most reliable, and the easiest faucets to repair are those in which the valve is screwed down onto the valve seat and water-tightness is made by inserting a rubber or leather washer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid self-closing and single-turn handle faucets where high pressure exists because packing wears quickly; nickel plating is an appearance choice only and increases cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitchen sink material: enameled iron is attractive but not functionally superior
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice lies between plain iron and enameled iron; an enameled iron sink costing $30 is very attractive but serves no more useful purpose than a $3 cast-iron sink and fifty-cent drainboard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose sink material according to budget and desired appearance; enameled iron with nickel faucets is ornamental but not necessarily more useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laundry tubs: prefer stationary enameled iron or slate tubs to wooden tubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Stationary tubs for laundry are worth their cost over movable wooden tubs in labor saved; wooden tubs absorb organic matter and have persistent odor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enameled iron tubs cost $20–$40 with fixtures; a set of three slate tubs costs ~$25; include piping for hot and cold, two faucets, and drain connections in budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-water boiler should have stop-cock and drain
rubrics_metrics.description: A stop-cock on the cold-water supply entering the tank is desirable so that if the tank bursts the cold water may be shut off; a drainpipe from the bottom is also desirable to draw off sediment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the galvanized iron kitchen boiler on its own stand and add piping and stop-cock; drain occasionally to remove sediment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tin-lined bath-tubs; prefer enameled iron or porcelain
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the old-fashioned tin-lined bath-tub—the lining rusts or corrodes and is difficult to keep clean; enameled iron tubs are preferable, and fancy porcelain offers no practical advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enameled iron tubs (e.g., 5.5 ft) cost $20–$100 without fixtures; choose durable, non-corroding materials over low first-cost tin linings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate cost: basic plumbing (excluding attic tank) ~ $150
rubrics_metrics.description: A fair estimate of the cost of plumbing in a house, including fixtures mentioned except the attic tank and including plumber's bill, is $150 with careful buying and no brass or nickel-plated piping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-grade fixtures including nickel fittings and nickel piping can raise fixture costs alone to ~$150 or more (not counting labor).

rubrics_metrics.name: House-drain material and diameter: vitrified tile, 5 inches inside
rubrics_metrics.description: The house-drain is generally made of vitrified tile and in ordinary practice is five inches inside diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower end discharges to cesspool, settling tank, or stream according to local conditions; see local regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lay house-drain straight with adequate grade (>= 1/4 in/ft)
rubrics_metrics.description: The house-drain should be carefully laid in a straight line both horizontally and vertically; such a pipe should have a grade of at least one quarter inch to a foot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straight runs have greater velocity reducing stoppage and are easier to clean; use a carpenter's level with a shim to set grade; joints made with Portland cement mixed with equal part sand and completely filled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide manhole near house for drain cleaning
rubrics_metrics.description: When nearing the house it is very desirable that a manhole should be built so that if a stoppage occurs it may be cleaned out without taking up the pipe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include manhole access in design to ease maintenance; in city houses include a running trap just outside with fresh-air inlet (but for a single house this may be omitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Soil-pipe: cast-iron, 4 inches diameter, run through roof
rubrics_metrics.description: The soil-pipe runs from the trap or cellar wall up through the roof so gases may escape and is generally of cast-iron (six-foot lengths) and almost always four inches inside diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Y fittings to connect fixtures; cover top with zinc netting to keep out leaves/birds; compute length from cellar to roof; estimate cost by weight plus fittings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support soil-pipe and especially elbows firmly
rubrics_metrics.description: The soil-pipe must be well supported along the cellar wall on brackets or hung from floor joists; special care must be taken to support the elbow where it turns upward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider building a brick pier from cellar bottom up to and around the elbow for firm support, especially for heavy lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make drainpipe joints with oakum and lead, then calk
rubrics_metrics.description: Joints in drainpipe should be made with oakum rammed into joints and then poured with sufficient melted lead to provide about an inch depth of joint; after cooling, expand or calk the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow standard lead jointing procedure to ensure watertightness and durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weatherproof roof penetration of soil-pipe with lead flashing
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent rain finding its way between soil-pipe and roof, wrap a piece of lead around the soil-pipe for about twelve inches above the roof and slip a flat piece of lead under the shingles soldered to the other piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly solder and seal lead flashing to avoid leaks and water intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixture-to-soil connections use lead pipe wiped on brass ferrule
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixtures are connected to the iron pipe usually by lead pipe, the lead pipe being first wiped onto a brass ferrule, the ferrule being leaded into the Y branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Y branches typically 2 inches and lead pipe about 1-1/4 inches; include a trap with ~1 inch water-seal between fixture and soil-pipe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trap vents optional in single houses; traps essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Vent pipes from top of trap to roof are customary in city plumbing but for a single house trap-vents seem hardly necessary; experiments show vent-pipes add cost with little benefit in some cases. Traps themselves are essential and should have a seal of about an inch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simplest effective trap (plain S trap) and include a clean-out at bottom (screw-plug) for clogged traps; ensure water-seal depth ~1 inch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose water-closet types that are simple, self-cleansing, and have safe seals
rubrics_metrics.description: Select closets which have the bowl and trap all in one piece, simple in construction, self-cleansing, and with safe water-seal; acceptable types include short-hopper, washout, washdown, syphonic, and syphon-jet, with washdown, syphon, and syphon-jet preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pan-closet and long-hopper closets which clog and allow decomposition; prefer washdown/syphon/syphon-jet for cleanliness and scouring action; syphonic and syphon-jet offer more powerful flushing and are relatively noiseless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not connect water-closet directly to small supply pipe; provide cistern for flushing
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct connection of closet to supply rim is objectionable because low pressure and concurrent flows may draw air or conceivably filth into supply; small house pipes may not deliver water fast enough for effective flushing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install a small copper-lined wooden tank (~3 gallons) above or back of closet, discharged through 1-1/4 inch pipe; tank costs about $10 and allows rapid discharge and float-valve refill avoiding direct dependence on main supply flow.
